wa_kettle_valley_curlew.blurb: Cliffs on both sides of the Kettle River, a few miles west of Curlew in rural Okanogan country. The rock is mainly granite, with patches of granodiorite and gneiss. Trad is the largest share, with a fair amount of sport, a set of boulders and a few top ropes. Routes are faces and cracks, some fully bolted and many mixed, needing a piece or two of gear, and they run from short pitches to roughly 300 feet. Grades follow older, traditional standards and cluster between 5.7 and 5.11. Morning Rock is the biggest wall, with a main face over 250 feet tall; The Bookstore, Viper Head and Shangri La add more crags.

bc_white_walls.blurb: A loose grouping of five crags within Skaha Bluffs, on a hillside above Skaha Lake just south of Penticton. The cliffs at Skaha are mainly gneiss, and the walls here face both east and west. Sport routes dominate, with a smaller number of trad lines. Grades are concentrated from 5.10 to 5.12, with some 5.13 and a thin scattering of easier climbs. Great White holds long, pumpy routes, while Little White is a wall of short technical lines that gets afternoon sun. Go Anywhere, Off White and Ochre Wall fill out the rest. The crags do not form one continuous cliff.

nh_wm_bartlett_jackson_area.blurb: A collection of small crags around Bartlett and Jackson in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. Trad and sport are close to evenly split, with a few boulder problems and an occasional ice line. Grades are mostly 5.8 to 5.11, with a handful of 5.12 and a few easy routes. Attitash Crag is the largest, mostly sport with some trad. Jackson Crag is also mainly sport, spread along a hillside in several sectors, and most of them are shaded in the early afternoon. Eagle Mountain Cliff holds both sport and trad, while White's Ledge and CMC Crag are mostly trad. Many of the others are small trad cliffs with only a few routes each.

nj_delaware_water_gap_nra.blurb: Climbing in northwest New Jersey, within the national recreation area along the Delaware River. Mount Tammany, at the southern end, holds almost all of it: single and multi-pitch trad on metaquartzite, with some bolts on sparsely protected stretches and bolted rappel stations. Ricks Rocks, at the northern end, offers top-rope and single-pitch climbing that is quick to reach and easy to set up. Small outcrops and slabs along the western side add some more. Trad is overwhelmingly the main style, with a few boulders, ice and aid lines. Grades start at the easiest fifth-class and run to 5.12, with most between 5.5 and 5.10.

ok_chandler_park.blurb: A limestone bouldering park on the west side of Tulsa, close to the Arkansas River. The boulders sit below the parking area, reached by stairs or a short gully scramble, and are grouped into the Autobahn Area, East Chandler and The New Old, with a few top ropes mixed in. Nearly all of the climbing is bouldering, with a wide grade range: many V0 to V5 problems, a solid middle at V6 to V8, and some harder ones up to V12. Landings are described as good, though holds can be polished smooth. Summer is very hot, but much of the area is shaded.
